title: Quantum feedback: theory, experiments, and applications
extended_summary:
This paper is a broad review of quantum feedback control rather than a study of educational intervention or any human-participant experiment. It asks how feedback can be formulated, analyzed, and implemented for quantum systems, with emphasis on the distinction between measurement-based feedback and coherent feedback.

The paper surveys the theoretical foundations of continuous quantum measurement, quantum filtering, quantum trajectories, Markovian feedback, Bayesian feedback, and coherent-feedback networks. It also discusses how feedback can be used for tasks such as noise reduction, state stabilization, squeezing, quantum error correction, entanglement control, and parameter estimation. The discussion is framed in control-theoretic terms and develops the relevant stochastic and input-output formalisms.

The contexts covered are physical laboratory systems such as quantum optics, trapped atoms and ions, superconducting circuits, optomechanical systems, and quantum dots. Because the article is a review, it synthesizes prior results and experimental demonstrations rather than reporting a single new dataset. Its main conclusion is that quantum feedback is a powerful control paradigm, with coherent feedback often offering advantages over measurement-based feedback in some settings, while measurement-based approaches remain important for direct state estimation and control.
